- `cloud`: number (default 1) — The cloud's size relative to the field's height, 0.4 to 1.6.
- `dotSize`: number (default 7) — Dot diameter, px, 3 to 12; the field fills its box with whole rows and columns.
- `pitch`: number (default 2.4) — Dot spacing as a multiple of the dot size.
- `drift`: number (default 1) — How fast the cloud drifts across, as a multiple of its natural pace.
- `swell`: number (default 0.5) — How much a shaded dot grows, 0 to 1.
- `dim`: number (default 0.55) — How much a shaded dot darkens toward the shade colour, 0 to 1.
- `sunColor`: string (default a warm pigment from --warn) — The dots in sunlight, any CSS colour; their highlight and rim are mixed from it.
- `shadeColor`: string (default a cool pigment from --accent-bright) — The dots in the cloud's shadow, any CSS colour.
- `label`: string (default "Working") — What the work is, spoken while busy (“Working…”).
- `labels`: Partial<Record<"idle" | "busy" | "done", string>> — What the status says in each state, replacing “Ready.”, “<label>…” and “Done.”.
- `seed`: number (default 3) — Shapes the clouds; each new cloud is a variation on it.
- `paused`: boolean (default false) — Hold the field as it is.
- `dpr`: number (default 2) — Device-pixel-ratio cap for the canvas, at most 2.
- `onSettle`: (state: "idle" | "busy" | "done") => void — Fires once a state's change has finished drawing — for done, when the field is fully lit.
- `className`: string (default "h-28") — Size the field with a height class.

Notes:
- Accessibility: the component is a polite status region whose text says the state (“Working…”, “Done.”, “Ready.” or your labels); the field is aria-hidden. It takes no input and never holds focus.
- Reduced motion: no cloud drifts — its shadow rests in the middle of the field and breathes by opacity alone while busy, and done still lifts the field to full sun.

- Usage: drive `state` from your request — busy while it runs, done when it returns — and keep it mounted; it costs nothing at rest.

### Flute Bubbles (KQ-1871) — `flute-bubbles`
Fine bubbles rising from points in the glass.

A tall flute of sparkling wine seen side-on: fine bubbles rise in steady strings from nucleation points on the walls and the point of the bowl, each born tiny, growing as it climbs and quickening with its size, catching the light on the way up and popping at the surface in a small ring that now and then flicks a droplet above the wine. Tapping the glass shivers its surface on springs.recoil and releases a burst of fresh streams from the wall nearest the press; left alone the wine slowly goes flat until Top up pours a thin stream in and a mousse swells on springs.glide and settles. The glass and Top up are real buttons, so Space and Enter tap the walls in turn and top it up.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/flute-bubbles`

Props:
- `streams`: number (default 7) — How many points on the glass give off a stream of bubbles, 2 to 16.
- `fizz`: number (default 0.6) — How lively the wine is, 0 (slow, sparse strings) to 1 (tight, quick ones).
- `tint`: "straw" | "rose" | "amber" | "water" (default "straw") — The wine's colour, a pigment that looks the same in both themes.
- `liquidColor`: string — Any CSS colour for the wine; it deepens toward the point of the bowl. Overrides tint.
- `fill`: number (default 0.8) — How full the bowl is, 0.5 to 0.92.
- `bubbleSize`: number (default 0.5) — Bubble size, 0 (the finest bead) to 1 (coarser).
- `glint`: number (default 0.7) — How brightly bubbles catch the light, 0 to 1.
- `burst`: number (default 0.6) — How many fresh streams a tap on the glass releases, 0 to 1.
- `flatAfter`: number (default 45000) — ms for the glass to go flat after a top-up; 0 keeps it lively for ever.
- `mousse`: boolean (default true) — A foam head swells on a top-up and settles.
- `onTap`: (side: "left" | "right" | "point") => void — Fires when the glass is tapped, with the wall the fresh streams rise from.
- `onTopUp`: () => void — Fires when the glass is topped up.
- `onFizzChange`: (state: "lively" | "settling" | "flat") => void — Fires when the wine turns lively, starts settling or goes flat.
- `sound`: boolean (default false) — A sizzle after each tap and top-up — only for the visitor's own press.
- `paused`: boolean (default false) — Hold every bubble where it is.
- `seed`: number (default 1) — Seeds where the streams start and how every bubble is born.
- `dpr`: number (default 2) — Cap on the canvas's device pixel ratio, at most 2.
- `label`: string (default "Glass of sparkling wine") — The glass's accessible name.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — The glass takes no taps and cannot be topped up.
- `className`: string (default "h-[30rem] w-full") — Sizes the piece; the flute keeps its shape and centres in it.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the glass is a button — Space or Enter taps it, alternating the left wall, the right wall and the point of the bowl; Top up is a second button. A polite status says where the fresh streams rose and when the glass goes flat.
- Reduced motion shows a still photograph of the glass: every stream frozen mid-rise. A tap redraws it with the fresh streams, a top-up shows the mousse for a moment, and nothing travels.
- Bubbles are a pooled 2D canvas (no allocation per frame) over crisp SVG glass; the loop runs only while the glass is on screen, the page visible and not paused, and the backing store is capped at `dpr`.
- The glass and the room are token colours and re-read on a theme change; the wine is pigment (fixed lightness from the warn, danger or accent hue) so it looks the same in light and dark.
- Give the piece a height: it is a size container and fits the 160 × 460 flute inside whatever box it gets.
- Sound is a single sizzle loop after each tap or top-up, only for the visitor's own press, and it always stops.

A scroll-linked stack: inside whatever scrolls it, each card slides up and files itself onto a tray near the top, and as the next card slides over it the filed card tilts a little to one side, sinks a hair and dims, so a small untidy pile grows above the card being read, every older card's top edge peeking above the next while the tray's label counts the pile. ### Thumb Flipbook (KQ-1879) — `thumb-flipbook`
Scroll to riffle the pages and the drawing moves.

A pocket flipbook lying on the table, taped at its spine, a thumb on the bottom-right corner holding the waiting pages' corners curled into a fan. Riffling lets the pages go one after another: each top page curls up past the thumb and turns away over the spine, revealing the next drawing, so the ink drawing in view moves (a boat on a rolling swell under a gull, a seamless loop) and a fast riffle keeps several pages in the air. Every page's peel springs toward the hand: the page under a drag tracks the finger on springs.flick and released pages flick past on springs.snap at the riffle rate, a flick coasts to where the throw would rest, and scrolling the page riffles forward and back; it is a slider, so arrows turn a page, Page Up and Page Down a loop, Home and End riffle to either end and Space riffles one loop.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/thumb-flipbook`

Props:
- `images`: string[] — One picture per frame, drawn on the pages in order; replaces the drawn loop.
- `frames`: number (default 12) — Drawings in the loop, 6 to 24: a choppy loop to a fluid one. Ignored with `images`.
- `pages`: number (default 48) — Pages in the book, 12 to 120.
- `bend`: number (default 0.6) — How far the thumb curls the waiting pages, 0 to 1: a slight lift to a tall fan.
- `riffle`: number (default 0.5) — Riffle speed, 0 to 1: a slow heavy peel to a quick flutter — pages per px of drag or scroll, and how fast each page flicks past.
- `value / defaultValue`: number (default — / 0) — Pages turned, 0 to `pages`, controlled or initial; a new value riffles to it.
- `onValueChange`: (page: number) => void — Fires from the drag, scroll or key that turned a page, with the pages turned.
- `scroll`: boolean (default true) — Scrolling the page (or any scroll container) riffles the book forward and back.
- `thumb`: boolean (default true) — Draw the thumb holding the pages.
- `paper`: string (default a warm white pigment) — The pages, any CSS colour.
- `ink`: string (default from the ink token at a fixed lightness) — The drawing's ink, any CSS colour.
- `accent`: string (default a red pigment from the danger token) — The drawing's one colour, any CSS colour.
- `sound`: boolean (default false) — A paper crinkle as each page leaves the thumb. Off unless asked for.
- `dpr`: number (default 2) — Cap on the canvas's device pixel ratio, at most 2.
- `label`: string (default "Flipbook") — The book's accessible name.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — No riffling by hand, scroll or key.
- `className`: string — Sizes the book's box; 8:5 and the full width by default.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the book is a slider (pages turned, with the drawing number in its value text); Right and Up turn a page, Left and Down turn back, Page Up and Page Down turn a whole loop, Home and End riffle to either end, Space or Enter riffles one loop.
- Reduced motion: pages change in place with no flight or curl spring, scrolling leaves the book alone, and keys and drags still turn whole pages; the book rests with a gentle held curl.
- Performance: Canvas 2D at a device pixel ratio capped at 2; page textures are drawn once per size and colour, each curled strip draws only its own slice, and the animation loop runs only while a page is in the air — never off screen or in a hidden tab.
- Scroll riffling reads how far the book moves on screen, so it works inside any scroll container or the page without configuration; turn it off with `scroll={false}`.
- Sound is silent until the visitor has clicked, tapped or pressed a key, since a scroll is not a user activation.

### Counter Dive (KQ-1880) — `counter-dive`
Scroll through the hole in a letter into the picture.

A giant word in a geometric monoline alphabet drawn in code, its strokes filled with a picture on a plain ground; as its scroll container scrolls through the section, the pinned stage magnifies the word around one letter's hole (the O of BROOK by default) and slides it to the middle of the frame. The hole is a window: the ground inside it thins away to show the picture beyond at its own depth, the strokes rush out past the edges as a flat ink, and you pass through into the picture, where the caption rises in; scrolling back pulls you out through the same hole. The shown progress follows the scroll on a critically damped spring with the springs.glide constants and the scale is exponential in progress, so the dive keeps a steady speed through depth; on the focused stage Down, Page Down and Space dive deeper, Up and Page Up back out, and Home and End jump to either end.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/counter-dive`

Props:
- `word`: string (default "BROOK") — The word, in capitals A–Z and spaces; other characters are dropped.
- `letter`: number | "auto" (default "auto") — Which letter to dive through, by its index in the word, or the most central letter with a hole.
- `weight`: number (default 0.5) — Stroke weight of the letters, 0 to 1: hairline letters with wide counters to heavy ones with portholes.
- `zoom`: number (default 90) — How far the word magnifies, 40 to 200: a gentle dive to a rush through the hole.
- `range`: number (default 900) — Scroll distance the dive takes, px (400 to 1600).
- `height`: number (default 480) — Height of the pinned stage, px. Give it the height of the scroll container it sits in.
- `src`: string (default a drawn valley at dusk) — The picture: in the letters, and beyond the hole.
- `alt`: string (default describes the drawn valley) — Describes the picture for assistive technology.
- `ground`: string (default "var(--background)") — The plain ground the word sits on, any CSS colour.
- `ink`: string (default a dusk pigment) — The flat colour the strokes become as they magnify past you, any CSS colour.
- `as`: "h1" | "h2" | "h3" (default "h2") — The element that carries the word for assistive technology.
- `children`: ReactNode — Shown in the picture once you are through.
- `onProgressChange`: (progress: number) => void — Fires as the dive progresses, 0 to 1, from the scroll that moved it.
- `onPhaseChange`: (phase: "word" | "diving" | "through") => void — Fires when the dive moves between the word, diving and through.
- `className`: string — Classes for the section; it takes the width of its column and the height of `height` plus `range`.

Notes:
- Place it inside the element that scrolls (an overflow-y: auto box, or the page) with no clipping ancestor in between: the stage pins with position: sticky and the dive reads that container's scroll. Set `height` to the container's visible height so the stage fills it.
- Keyboard: the stage is focusable; Down, Page Down and Space dive deeper, Up and Page Up back out, Home and End jump to the start or the end by scrolling the container, so pointer and keyboard reach the same states. Arriving in the picture and returning to the word are announced politely.
- Accessibility: the word is a real heading (visually hidden; the SVG is decoration) and `alt` describes the picture.
- Reduced motion: nothing zooms; the word holds still and, past half the range, the picture and the caption cross-fade in over it, and back out before half.
- Performance: one SVG; each frame writes only the transforms and opacities that changed, rounded, and the smoothing loop stops as soon as the dive catches up with the scroll; nothing runs off screen.

### Peg Migration (KQ-1881) — `peg-migration`
Pegs hop hole to hole to make the next picture.

A backlit pegboard whose translucent coloured pegs glow with the light behind the board and make a picture: a drawn one, a word in a 5 × 7 peg alphabet, or any image reduced to pegs. To change pictures the pegs migrate: pegs already right stay put, the rest are matched to the nearest hole that needs their colour and travel there hole to hole in up to five short arcs, leaving the light and casting a shadow as they lift and landing with a flash and the springs.recoil squash, their departures staggered by distance from where you clicked so the board changes in a wave while spare pegs hop off the nearer side and new ones hop in. A click, Enter, Space or Right shows the next picture, Left the previous, and Home and End the first and last.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/peg-migration`

Props:
- `images`: { alt: string; src?: string; text?: string; color?: number; draw?: (u: number, v: number, aspect: number) => number }[] (default a sun on the sea, a koi, a moon over a ridge, a tulip) — The pictures, in order: an image reduced to pegs, a word in the peg alphabet, or a drawing function returning a colour index (or -1) for each hole.
- `value / defaultValue`: number (default — / 0) — The picture showing, controlled or initial.
- `onValueChange`: (index: number) => void — Fires from the click or key that asked for another picture.
- `pitch`: number (default 13) — Distance between holes, px (9 to 21): a fine board to a chunky toy.
- `hopSpeed`: number (default 1) — How quickly pegs hop, 0.5 to 2.
- `glow`: number (default 0.6) — How far each peg's light blooms around it, 0 to 1.
- `colors`: string[] (default seven pigments from the tokens) — The peg colours, any CSS colours; pictures index into them.
- `board`: string (default a near-black pigment) — The board's colour, any CSS colour.
- `hopHeight`: number (default 0.5) — How high pegs arc as they hop, 0 to 1.
- `spread`: number (default 0.5) — How long the wave takes to cross the board, 0 (all at once) to 1 (a slow sweep).
- `interval`: number (default 0) — Moves to the next picture on its own every so many ms while on screen and not hovered or focused; 0 never.
- `seed`: number (default 1) — Seeds the small differences in each peg's timing.
- `sound`: boolean (default false) — A tick as each peg lands, pitched by its colour. Off unless asked for.
- `dpr`: number (default 2) — Cap on the canvas's device pixel ratio, at most 2.
- `label`: string (default "Pegboard") — The board's accessible name.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — No changing pictures.
- `className`: string — Sizes the board; 3:1 and the full width by default.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the board is one focusable group named with the picture it shows; Enter, Space or Right shows the next picture (Right sweeps from the left edge), Left the previous, Home and End the first and last. The new picture is announced politely.
- Reduced motion: no hops; the old picture fades out where it stands and the new one fades in, because the picture is the information.
- Performance: Canvas 2D at a device pixel ratio capped at 2; the board and every peg and glow sprite are drawn once per size and colour, a settled board is one blit, and the loop runs only while pegs are moving — never off screen or in a hidden tab. Auto-advance pauses off screen, in a hidden tab, and while hovered or focused.
- Images are reduced on the client: each hole samples the picture and takes the nearest peg colour, and dark or transparent areas leave holes empty, so a high-contrast image on black reads best. Images from another origin need CORS.
- Text uses a 5 × 7 peg alphabet, doubled when the board is big enough and set in 3 × 5 when it is narrow.

### Second Contact (KQ-1882) — `second-contact`
Drag the moon over the sun and wait for the ring.

A solar eclipse you drive: drag the dark moon (anywhere on the sky moves it 1:1; a tap glides it there on springs.glide) and as it covers more of the sun the sky deepens through twilight to night, a ring of sunset lights the horizon and stars come out. The moon's limb is a seeded profile of mountains and valleys, so near totality the last crescent breaks into Baily's beads of light through the valleys, then one diamond ring with the inner corona already showing, then totality: a pearly corona with long helmet streamers and fine striations drifting in colour around the hue, and pink prominences on the limb. One WebGL2 pass draws the scene while the light is measured on the CPU (the visible share of the disc, and the gaps at 720 angles round the limb gathered into beads); the moon is a slider of how much of the sun is covered, so arrow keys move it in fine steps near the sun, Home sets it at totality and End back where it began, and releasing leaves it where it is.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/second-contact`

Props:
- `value / defaultValue`: { x: number; y: number } (default — / { x: -0.95, y: 0.28 }) — Where the moon's centre is, in sun radii from the sun's centre, y down; controlled or initial.
- `onValueChange`: (point: { x: number; y: number }) => void — Fires from the drag, tap or key that moved the moon.
- `onPhaseChange`: (phase: "clear" | "partial" | "beads" | "diamond" | "totality") => void — Fires when the eclipse moves between clear, partial, beads, the diamond ring and totality.
- `corona`: number (default 0.6) — How far the corona reaches, 0 to 1: a tight bright collar to streamers past three radii.
- `beads`: number (default 0.7) — How bright the last light is, 0 to 1: faint pinpricks to blazing beads and a big diamond.
- `hue`: number (default 200) — The corona's tint, a hue in degrees.
- `sunSize`: number (default 0.21) — The sun's radius as a share of the shorter side, 0.12 to 0.32.
- `prominences`: number (default 0.5) — How many pink prominences stand on the limb at totality, 0 to 1.
- `stars`: boolean (default true) — Stars come out as the sky darkens.
- `sky`: string (default a pigment from the accent token) — The daytime sky, any CSS colour.
- `night`: string (default a deep blue pigment) — The sky at totality, any CSS colour.
- `shimmer`: number (default 0.4) — How much the beads and the corona shimmer, 0 to 1.
- `seed`: number (default 7) — Seeds the moon's mountains and valleys and the corona's streamers.
- `dpr`: number (default 2) — Cap on the canvas's device pixel ratio, at most 2.
- `label`: string (default "Eclipse") — The scene's accessible name.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — No dragging or keys.
- `className`: string — Sizes the scene; it fills its parent by default.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the moon is a focusable slider whose value is the share of the sun covered, with the phase in its value text; arrow keys move it in their direction (in fine steps near the sun, where the beads and the ring are, and big steps with Shift), Home sets it at totality and End back where it began. Phase changes are announced politely.
- Reduced motion: the scene is still — no corona drift and no shimmer — and a tap moves the moon at once instead of gliding; the moon still follows a drag 1:1 and every phase still renders.
- Performance: one WebGL2 pass at a 0.75 render scale on dense screens with the device pixel ratio capped at 2; it draws only when the moon moves, plus a slow loop while the corona or beads show on screen. Context loss is handled and the scene redraws on restore; without WebGL2 a CSS scene of sky, sun, corona and moon follows the same value and phases.
- Give it a height: it fills its parent, and the sun's size is a share of the shorter side, so it suits a square card or a wide hero.

### Room Within (KQ-1883) — `room-within`
Scroll into a window that holds the next room.

A story told as one long zoom: the stage is its own scroll container, each picture holds an opening exactly the stage's shape, and scrolling zooms into it until it fills the stage and becomes the next picture, which holds the next opening. The camera is one transform written straight from the scroll — a pure geometric scale about the opening's fixed point, so it grows from one steady spot and every level boundary is seamless — while the glass sheen slides off the window, the far room's haze lifts and the captions cross-fade with the zoom; a click on the opening, the depth gauge or Page Down travels there on springs.drift. Page Down, Space and Enter go in a level, Page Up, Shift+Space and Backspace come back out, Home and End jump to the ends.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/room-within`

Props:
- `items`: RoomWithinLevel[] (default defaultRoomWithinLevels) — The pictures, outermost first, each { id?, src?, alt, caption?, detail?, art?, window? }; each one's opening holds the next.
- `depth`: number (default 5) — How many levels deep the story goes, 2 to 6 (and no more than items).
- `frame`: "window" | "gilt" | "mat" | "none" (default "window") — How each opening is framed: a painted casement with a sill, a gilt frame, a paper mat, or a seamless cut.
- `easing`: "linear" | "dwell" | "snap" (default "dwell") — How scrolling maps to the zoom: steady, holding each picture still for a beat, or snapping every scroll to a picture.
- `value / defaultValue`: number (default — / 0) — The level shown. A new controlled value travels there.
- `onValueChange`: (level: number) => void — Fires from the scroll, key or click that brought a new level nearest, with that level.
- `scrollLength`: number (default 1.2) — Scroll for one level, as a share of the stage's height, 0.5 to 3.
- `loop`: boolean (default true) — The deepest picture's opening holds the first room again.
- `captions`: boolean (default true) — Show each level's caption and detail over the picture.
- `rail`: boolean (default true) — Show the depth gauge on the right edge; its ticks travel to a level.
- `hint`: boolean (default true) — On first view the camera leans a little way into the window and back, and a cue says to scroll.
- `height`: number | string (default 420px) — The stage's height: px, or any CSS length. A className height works too.
- `label`: string (default "Room within") — The story's accessible name.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — No scrolling, keys or clicks; the stage dims.
- `className`: string — Classes for the stage.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the stage is a focusable region (aria-roledescription "zooming story"); Page Down, Space and Enter travel one level in, Page Up, Shift+Space and Backspace one level out, Home and End to the ends, digits 1–9 to a level, and the arrow keys scroll natively in small steps. A polite live region announces "Level 2 of 5: Across the courtyard." as each level arrives.
- Reduced motion: no zoom — the pictures cross-fade full-frame at the same scroll positions, the current picture's opening still shows the next one, and keyed or clicked travel jumps at once.
- Performance: there is no animation loop. The camera, glass, haze, captions and gauge are written straight from scroll events; motion animates only a keyed or clicked travel. At most five pictures are in the DOM, as flat siblings laid into each other by CSS, so moving deeper never remounts one.
- Openings (window: { x, y, size }) are placed in the art's 1000 × 1000 box, which is a square covering the stage, and keep the stage's aspect, so the zoom is seamless from a 316px phone to a 1200px plate and the server's first paint is already right.
- Wheel and touch scrolling inside the stage drive the story and chain on to the page at either end; give it a height in the layout (height prop or a className) since it is its own scroll container.

### Zellige Wall (KQ-1884) — `zellige-wall`
A picture set in glazed tiles that tilt to light.

A picture rebuilt from small glazed tiles, each an unevenly cut square set a hair askew in grout, its colour box-averaged from the picture and pulled toward the picture's own glazes, lit per pixel in one instanced WebGL2 draw with a pillowed face, a rolled rim that catches the light and a hairline of bare clay. Every tile has its own tilt spring, between the springs.snap and springs.recoil constants by wobble: tiles under the pointer lean toward it so a ring of glints follows the hand and rings back as it passes, and a click sends a ripple across the whole wall that kicks each tile outward as the front reaches it. Arrow keys move a keyboard lamp the tiles lean toward, and Enter or Space sends the ripple from it.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/zellige-wall`

Props:
- `src`: string — A picture to set in tiles (same-origin, or served with CORS). Without one, a drawn courtyard door is used.
- `alt`: string (default a description of the drawn courtyard) — Describes the picture.
- `tile`: number (default 14) — Tile size, px, 8 to 28.
- `glaze`: number (default 0.6) — Glaze shine, 0 (matte clay) to 1 (wet glass): the strength and tightness of every highlight.
- `tilt`: number (default 18) — How far a tile leans toward the pointer, degrees, 0 to 35.
- `radius`: number (default 90) — How far from the pointer tiles lean, px.
- `rippleSpeed`: number (default 520) — How fast a click's ripple crosses the wall, px per second.
- `wobble`: number (default 0.5) — How the tiles settle, 0 (one crisp overshoot, springs.snap) to 1 (a ringing wobble, springs.recoil).
- `jitter`: number (default 0.5) — How unevenly the tiles are cut, 0 (machine-square) to 1 (hand-cut).
- `askew`: number (default 2.5) — How far a tile is set off square, degrees.
- `grout`: string (default a mix of the page background and ink) — The grout between the tiles, any CSS colour.
- `light`: number (default -135) — The key light's direction, degrees (−135 is from the upper left).
- `interactive`: boolean (default true) — Tiles answer the pointer and keys; off, the wall is a still picture with role="img".
- `seed`: number (default 7) — Seeds the cut and set of every tile.
- `dpr`: number (default 2) — Cap on the canvas's device pixel ratio, at most 2.
- `onRipple`: (origin: { x: number; y: number }) => void — Fires from the click or key that sent a ripple, with its origin as shares of the wall (0–1).
- `label`: string (default "Glazed tile wall") — The wall's accessible name.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — No pointer, clicks or keys; the wall dims.
- `className`: string — Sizes the wall; it fills its parent by default.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the wall is a focusable group (aria-roledescription "tile wall"); the arrow keys move a lamp the tiles lean toward, exactly as they do to the pointer, Home recentres it, and Enter or Space sends the ripple from it. A polite live region says where each ripple came from; the picture's alt is read once.
- Reduced motion: no tile ever tilts or rings — the wall is a still glazed mosaic; the pointer's lamp still lights a soft glint where it is, and a click or Enter brightens the glaze briefly instead of sending a wave.
- Performance: one instanced draw (plus a shadow pass) for every tile; tilts live in a Float32Array uploaded with bufferSubData. The loop runs only while tiles move or a ripple travels, on screen and visible, and stops on a settled frame. DPR is capped, context loss is handled, and without WebGL2 the server's still — the picture under a grout grid — stays.
- A src picture must be readable back (same origin or CORS); if it is not, the wall falls back to the drawn courtyard. Tiles are pulled less toward the palette for your own pictures so their colours survive.
- The grout follows the page theme (re-read on a theme change); the glazes are pigments, so the mosaic itself looks the same on a light or a dark page.

### Thought Avalanche (KQ-1885) — `thought-avalanche`
Seed a thought and watch how far it spreads.

A dark field of a few hundred nodes joined by faint, bowed filaments, where a click fires the nearest node and each firing sends glowing pulses on to its neighbours with a chance set by the branching ratio — counted over the neighbours that are not still resting — so an avalanche fizzles out below 1, swings between a handful and most of the field near it, and storms across everything above it. Pulses run along the curves at the conduction speed with short bright tails, the filaments they crossed keep an afterglow, fired nodes flash and then rest for the refractory time, and a ring blooms on the clicked node on the springs.snap constants. Arrow keys move a selection ring from node to node, Home returns it to the middle, and Enter or Space fires it.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/thought-avalanche`

Props:
- `branching`: number (default 1.1) — How many neighbours a firing sets off on average, 0.5 (fizzles) to 2 (storms); about 1 is critical.
- `refractory`: number (default 1600) — How long a fired node rests before it can fire again, ms.
- `hue`: number (default 195) — The glow's hue, degrees 0–360; the dark field takes a trace of it.
- `density`: number (default 14) — Nodes per 100 × 100 px of field, 2 to 40.
- `connections`: number (default 5) — Each node's nearest neighbours it is joined to, 2 to 8.
- `conduction`: number (default 240) — How fast a pulse runs along a filament, px per second.
- `glow`: number (default 0.7) — How bright the pulses, afterglow and flashes are, 0 to 1.
- `intro`: boolean (default true) — The first time the field is in view, one avalanche starts by itself; it is silent and reports nothing.
- `spontaneous`: number (default 0) — Stray firings a minute while the field is in view, 0 for none.
- `paused`: boolean (default false) — Freeze every pulse where it is.
- `seed`: number (default 3) — Seeds the network's layout and the chances.
- `dpr`: number (default 2) — Cap on the canvas's device pixel ratio, at most 2.
- `onAvalanche`: (stats: ThoughtAvalancheStats) => void — Fires as a visitor's avalanche starts, at each new generation, and when it ends, with { size, reach, generations, active, phase: "spreading" | "fizzled" | "faded" | "storm" }.
- `label`: string (default "Thought field") — The field's accessible name.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — No clicks or keys; the field dims.
- `className`: string — Sizes the field; it fills its parent by default.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the field is a focusable group (aria-roledescription "thought field"); a keyboard focus shows a selection ring on the middle node, the arrow keys move it to the nearest node in that direction, Home brings it back, and Enter or Space fires it. A polite live region announces each avalanche once, when it ends: "48 thoughts over 6 steps, spread and faded."
- Reduced motion: nothing travels — a firing resolves the whole cascade at once and draws its map (every node that fired and every filament it used) over the field, which holds and then fades on a CSS opacity transition; the sizes and steps still report.
- Performance: Canvas 2D with the faint network painted once per size and colour; a frame draws only lit filaments, live pulses (a preallocated typed-array pool) and node flashes (one pre-rendered glow sprite). The loop runs only while something is lit or resting, on screen and visible, and stops after; DPR is capped.
- The field is always dark — a night panel in both themes — with the glow from hue; give it a size (it fills its parent). A seeded thought always reaches at least one neighbour, so a click never does nothing; after that the branching ratio decides.
- Within one avalanche a node tires (each further firing passes on half as much), so even a storm ends; spontaneous firings run on a timer only while the field is in view.

### Planetarium Roof (KQ-1886) — `planetarium-roof`
Lie back and drag a ceiling of pictures.

A gallery seen from the floor of a planetarium: prints pinned to the inside of a dome overhead in loose constellations of three, over a faint graticule, pricked stars and constellation lines, each print posed by the Jacobian of an equisolid fisheye at its centre so the ones near the edge compress and turn as the dome curves away. Dragging turns the whole dome 1:1 under the finger and a release coasts on with the throw's velocity, decaying by inertia, while keyboard moves turn it to each print on the springs.glide constants. Clicking a print flies it down into focus — its pose decomposed into rotation, scales, shear and centre and tweened to an upright, centred print on springs.glide as the dome dims and the caption rises — and Escape, Close or a click on the dome flies it home.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/planetarium-roof`

- `fov`: number (default 110) — Field of view across the dome, degrees, 70 to 150: a close dome or a wide sweep.
- `spacing`: number (default 1) — How far apart the constellations and their prints sit, 0.6 to 1.6.
- `inertia`: number (default 0.6) — How long a throw coasts, 0 (stops dead) to 1 (coasts long).
- `value / defaultValue`: number | null (default — / null) — The print in focus, or null for none.
- `onValueChange`: (index: number | null) => void — Fires from the click or key that brought a print into focus or sent it back.
- `drift`: number (default 1.2) — How fast the dome turns by itself while idle, degrees a second; 0 holds it still.
- `altitude`: number (default 84) — Where the view starts, degrees above the horizon (90 looks straight up).
- `cardSize`: number (default 17) — Each print's width on the dome, degrees.
- `graticule`: boolean (default true) — Draw the dome's altitude rings and meridians.
- `lines`: boolean (default true) — Join each constellation's prints with thin lines.
- `stars`: number (default 140) — How many stars are pricked into the dome.
- `seed`: number (default 4) — Seeds the constellations' shapes and the stars.
- `height`: number (default 480) — The stage's height, px.
- `label`: string (default "Planetarium gallery") — The gallery's accessible name.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — No turning, clicks or keys; the dome dims.
- `className`: string — Classes for the stage.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the prints are buttons with one tab stop (roving tabindex) inside a region with aria-roledescription "carousel"; Left and Right move between prints, Up and Down between constellations, Home and End to the first and last, and the dome turns to each. Enter or Space brings a print into focus and moves focus to Close; Left and Right switch prints in focus; Escape (handled, so the page never sees it) sends it back and returns focus to its print.
- Reduced motion: the dome never drifts or coasts and keyboard moves turn it at once; a drag still turns it 1:1 under the finger, and a print in focus cross-fades in at the centre instead of flying.
- Performance: one loop that runs only while the dome moves (a coast, a keyboard turn, or drift), on screen and visible; it writes each print's CSS matrix directly and redraws a small Canvas 2D layer of rings, stars and lines (DPR-capped). With drift 0 it is idle until touched.
- The dome takes the page's surfaces and ink, so it is a pale plaster ceiling on a light page and a night sky on a dark one; the prints are pigment art or your src images, and the server renders every print already posed.
- Touch turns the dome horizontally and leaves vertical swipes to the page (touch-action pan-y); mouse and pen turn it both ways.

### Slot Canyon (KQ-1887) — `slot-canyon`
Fly the narrow slot, lit from a crack of sky.

An endless flight down a narrow sandstone slot canyon, raymarched in one WebGL2 pass: the walls are a distance field around a meandering centreline whose lean changes with height, so the slot winds one way at the floor and another overhead, banded with strata and carved with flowing flutes, glowing with light bounced down from a thin crack of sky — warm high up, violet-brown below. Where the crack opens, sun falls in shafts gathered by a short volumetric march through drifting dust, so the beams hang in the air and light the floor where they land. The pointer steers sideways and up toward the crack on the springs.glide constants, banking the camera so the canyon twists around you, and drifts home on springs.drift when it leaves; the arrow keys steer the same way, Home recentres and Space pauses the flight.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/slot-canyon`

Props:

- `width`: number (default 1) — How wide the slot is, 0.6 (a squeeze) to 1.4 (a wider passage).
- `shafts`: number (default 0.6) — Sunlight through the crack, 0 (none) to 1 (bright shafts and lit floor).
- `steer`: number (default 0.7) — How far the pointer and arrow keys steer, 0 to 1.
- `twist`: number (default 0.6) — How much the camera banks with the steer and the slot's own bends, 0 to 1.
- `dust`: number (default 0.5) — Dust hanging and glinting in the shafts, 0 to 1.
- `strata`: number (default 0.6) — How strongly the rock is banded, 0 (plain) to 1 (bold strata).
- `colors`: [string, string, string] (default sandstone pigments from the warn, danger and accent tokens) — The lit rock, the shade, and the sky, as CSS colours.
- `paused / defaultPaused`: boolean (default — / false) — The flight holds where it is.
- `onPausedChange`: (paused: boolean) => void — Fires from the Space key that paused or resumed the flight.
- `seed`: number (default 2) — Seeds the canyon's course and its cracks.
- `dpr`: number (default 2) — Cap on the canvas's device pixel ratio, at most 2.
- `label`: string (default "Slot canyon flight") — The scene's accessible name.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — No steering or keys.
- `className`: string — Sizes the scene; it fills its parent by default.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the scene is a focusable group (aria-roledescription "canyon flight"); the arrow keys steer left and right and look up and down exactly as the pointer does, Home recentres, and Space pauses and resumes the flight (announced politely). Children above it stay interactive and keep their own keys.
- Reduced motion: one still frame from a fixed place in the canyon — no flight, no drifting dust; the arrow keys still turn the view and redraw it once.
- Performance: the raymarch renders at half (DPR ≥ 1.5) or three-quarter scale with DPR capped; the loop runs only while flying or the steer settles, on screen and visible, and stops when paused. Context loss is handled, and without WebGL2 (and on the server) an SVG still of layered strata walls under a shaft stands in.
- The canyon is painted from pigments, so it looks the same on a light or a dark page; pass colors to recolour the rock, the shade and the sky. A wide stage looks through a longer lens so the slot keeps its depth.
- Give it a size (it fills its parent) and put your hero copy in children with a text shadow; the walls run dark at the bottom, where copy reads best.

### Switchback Trails (KQ-1888) — `switchback-trails`
Hold the shutter over a winding mountain road.

A dusk view across a valley to a mountain road zigzagging down a slope in hairpins, its legs smaller and thinner the higher they climb, with cars driving it both ways — warm-white headlights coming down, red tail lights going up — slowing into every hairpin. Press and hold to open the shutter: an iris opens on the springs.snap constants, a readout counts the seconds, and each car's lights are drawn from where they were to where they are into an additive exposure layer, so white and red trails build along the hairpins, brightest where the cars slow, while the sky lifts as a long exposure does. Release and the iris closes on the exit ease as the photograph develops with a halation bloom, holds, and slowly fades; Space opens it while held, Enter toggles it, Escape closes it.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/switchback-trails`

Props:
- `exposure`: number (default 0) — Exposure compensation, EV −2 (faint streaks) to +2 (blown rivers of light): how fast light builds and how wide the trails bloom.
- `traffic`: number (default 0.5) — How busy the road is, 0 (an empty pass) to 1 (a steady stream).
- `dusk`: number (default 0.55) — The light, 0 (last warm light) to 1 (deep blue hour with stars).
- `open / defaultOpen`: boolean (default — / false) — The shutter is open.
- `onOpenChange`: (open: boolean) => void — Fires from the press, release or key that opened or closed the shutter.
- `onExpose`: (shot: { seconds: number; cars: number }) => void — Fires as the shutter closes, with how long it was open and how many cars drew a trail.
- `fade`: number (default 6000) — How long the developed photograph takes to fade back to the live view, ms.
- `develop`: boolean (default true) — The halation bloom that swells as the photograph develops.
- `speed`: number (default 1) — How fast the cars drive, 0.5 to 2.
- `maxExposure`: number (default 30) — The shutter closes by itself after this long, seconds.
- `lightColors`: [string, string] (default warm white and red pigments) — Headlights and tail lights, CSS colours.
- `stars`: boolean (default true) — Stars come out as the dusk deepens.
- `paused`: boolean (default false) — Hold the live traffic still (an open shutter still records).
- `seed`: number (default 5) — Seeds the mountains, the traffic and the stars.
- `dpr`: number (default 2) — Cap on the canvas's device pixel ratio, at most 2.
- `label`: string (default "Hold to open the shutter") — The control's accessible name.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — No pressing or keys; the view dims.
- `className`: string — Sizes the view; it fills its parent by default.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the view is a role="button" with aria-pressed for the shutter; Space opens it while held and closes it on release (repeats are ignored), Enter opens and closes it for anyone who cannot hold a key, and Escape closes an open shutter (handled, so the page never sees it). A polite live region announces each photograph once: "Exposure 4.6 seconds, 9 cars."
- Reduced motion: no moving lights in the live view; holding the shutter fades in a finished long exposure (the trails laid down at once) more fully the longer you hold, and release holds the photograph and fades it out — no bloom, and the iris cross-fades.
- Performance: the dusk scene is painted once per size, tone and theme into an offscreen canvas; a frame is three drawImage calls and a short line per car (typed arrays, no per-frame allocation). Live traffic draws at 30 frames a second only while on screen and visible; an exposure or a fading photograph draws every frame; paused with the shutter closed and the photograph gone, nothing runs.
- A press holds the shutter open until the pointer lifts anywhere on the page; a touch that turns into a scroll closes it. The view is painted from pigments, so the dusk looks the same on a light or a dark page; the server renders a still with the road and a pair of trails.
- Give it a size (it fills its parent); in a cropped box the sky gives way first so the hairpins stay in view.

### Wing Scales (KQ-1889) — `wing-scales`
Iridescent ridges of a wing, shifting as you tilt.

A specimen of an invented blue butterfly drawn per pixel in one WebGL2 pass, zoomable from the whole insect down to the ridges of a single scale: rows of toothed scales laid like shingles, coloured by a thin-film term on their ridges, so the blue slides toward green and violet as the pointer rocks the specimen on a critically damped spring with the drift constants. The wheel (once focused), a pinch, double-click or the keys zoom about the pointer on the glide constants in log space; zoomed in, a drag pans 1:1 and a release throws by projection, and while you look the scales breathe in a slow wave that settles when you leave. Plus and minus zoom, Home and End jump to the wing or the ridges, Left and Right rock it, Shift with an arrow pans, and Escape returns to the whole wing.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/wing-scales`

Props:

- `maxZoom`: number (default 90) — The deepest magnification, 8 to 160.
- `iridescence`: number (default 0.75) — How strongly the ridges shine, 0 (dull pigment brown) to 1 (the full blue-green play).
- `tilt`: number (default 0.6) — How far the wing rocks toward the pointer, 0 (held still) to 1 (26° each way).
- `film`: number (default 420) — Thickness of the ridges' film in nanometres, 300 to 560: the colour family (gold, violet, blue, green).
- `ground`: string (default "oklch(0.26 0.03 45)") — The pigment under the film, any CSS colour.
- `markings`: "band" | "eyespot" | "plain" (default "band") — The pattern of pigment scales: a spotted outer band, an eyespot on each hindwing, or plain.
- `breathe`: number (default 0.5) — How far the scales lift as the wing breathes while you look, 0 to 1.
- `wheel`: "focus" | "always" | "off" (default "focus") — When a plain wheel zooms: once the wing has focus (or with Ctrl or ⌘), always, or never. Pinch always zooms.
- `seed`: number (default 7) — Seeds the scales' small irregularities.
- `label`: string (default "Butterfly wing") — Names the specimen for assistive technology.
- `paused`: boolean (default false) — Holds the scales flat: no breathing.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — Shows the wing but takes no gestures or keys.
- `dpr`: number (default 2) — Cap on the canvas's device pixel ratio, at most 2.
- `className`: string — Sizes the box (default h-56 w-full); the insect is fitted inside it.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the wing is one focusable group — + and − (or Up and Down) zoom, Page Up and Page Down by ×3, Home the whole wing, End the ridges, Enter the next level, Left and Right rock it toward the light, Shift with an arrow pans, and Escape (handled only while zoomed) returns to ×1. A polite status reads the magnification when it settles.
- Wheel etiquette: with wheel="focus" a plain wheel scrolls the page until the wing is clicked or focused (a hint says so); once it is, scrolling down looks deeper toward the ridges and up backs out. Ctrl or ⌘ with the wheel, and trackpad pinches, always zoom (spread to zoom in); at either zoom limit the wheel returns to the page. Touch pinches zoom, and the page still scrolls vertically over an unzoomed wing.
- Reduced motion: no breathing, no tilt following the pointer and no glides — zoom, pan and key tilts change in place — while the colour and the magnification still show.
- Performance: one fullscreen triangle with no textures, drawn only while a spring, the breath or a gesture is moving, on screen and with the tab visible; DPR is capped at `dpr`, context loss rebuilds, and without WebGL2 (and as the server's first frame) an SVG still of the same insect is shown.
- Theming: the insect is fixed pigment art on a transparent canvas with a black-alpha shadow, so it sits on any card in light or dark; `ground` accepts tokens and is re-read when the theme changes.

Pictures on a paper scroll rolling away overhead.

- `onProgressChange`: (progress: number) => void — Fires as the paper rolls, 0 (all hanging) to 1 (rolled to the last picture).

### Drying Line (KQ-1891) — `drying-line`
Prints pegged on a line, twisting as it pulls past.

Darkroom prints pegged to a sagging cord under a red safelight, on a pulley loop you pull past: a drag follows 1:1 and commits by projection to the nearest print on the glide spring with the release velocity, and the page's scroll pulls it too. Every print is a real pendulum and a torsion pendulum, swung about its peg by the line's acceleration and twisted by the air each its own way, damped by `sway`, so the glossy faces turn and a band of red light slides across them before they hang still and the loop stops. Clicking a print unclips it: the jaw opens on the flick spring and the print glides to the front with its darkroom note, and Back on the line or Escape carries it back as the jaw snaps shut on snap; Left and Right pull the line a print, Home and End go to the ends.

- `sway`: number (default 0.5) — How freely the prints swing and twist, 0 (stiff, quickly still) to 1 (loose, long and wide).
- `sag`: number (default 0.45) — How deep the cord sags between its hooks, 0 (taut) to 1 (a deep curve).

- `scroll`: boolean (default true) — The page's scroll (or the nearest scroll container's) pulls the line too.
- `light`: string (default "oklch(0.66 0.19 32)") — The safelight's colour, any CSS colour.

- Gestures: a horizontal drag with `touch-action: pan-y`, so the page still scrolls vertically on touch; a sideways wheel or trackpad swipe over the room pulls the line, and with `scroll` the page's own scroll winds it half as far without ever being taken from the page.

- Performance: DOM and SVG with one rAF loop writing transforms to the print nodes only while the line, a pendulum or a peg is moving, on screen and with the tab visible; it stops at rest. The page-scroll listener is passive.
- The room is fixed darkroom art (a warm near-black wall, the safelight's glow, prints tinted by its light), so it reads the same on a light or dark page; `light` changes the lamp and the tint together.

- `stagger`: number (default 0.5) — How far apart the slates of a course land, 0 (together) to 1 (one by one across).
- `cut`: "square" | "round" | "point" (default "square") — The shape of each slate's tail.
- `startCourses`: number (default 2) — How many courses are on before any scroll, 0 to 3.
- `paint`: string (default "oklch(0.97 0.01 90)") — The colour of the sign paint, a concrete CSS colour (the paint is an image, so not a var).
- `range`: number (default 900) — Scroll distance for the whole roof, px.
- `height`: number (default 520) — Height of the pinned stage, px; give it the height of the scroll container it sits in.
- `sound`: boolean (default false) — Play a clack as each slate lands.
- `onCoursesChange`: (laid: number) => void — Fires with the number of whole courses laid, from the scroll or key that changed it.
- `onProgressChange`: (progress: number) => void — Fires as the roof is laid, 0 to 1.
- `className`: string — Classes for the section.

Notes:
- Place it inside a scroll container (or the page) and give `height` that container's visible height: the section is height + range tall and its stage sticks while the courses go on. The headline is chalked on the felt before any slate is laid, so the first frame always reads.
- Keyboard: the roof is one focusable group — Down, Page Down and Space lay the next course, Up and Page Up lift the top one, Home and End lift all or lay all — by scrolling the container. The headline is a real heading and the picture's description is sr-only; a polite status says how many courses are laid and when the roof is complete.
- Reduced motion: no flights, settles or sheen; slates appear in place course by course on an opacity fade and fade out when lifted, while the count and callbacks still update.
- Sound: `clack` as slates land, panned to where they land and played only after the visitor has clicked, tapped or pressed a key on the page (a scroll is not an activation); one per course under reduced motion.
- Performance: DOM slates sharing two background images through CSS variables (the paint SVG is regenerated only on resize or a new headline); one passive, frame-coalesced scroll listener; the laid count is the only state the scroll changes, and animations run only while slates are in flight.

### Raking Light (KQ-1895) — `raking-light`
A low light that skims the surface for texture.

An object on a light table, relit per pixel in WebGL2 by a lamp that lies low at its side, so the light skims the surface and every ridge throws a long shadow marched through a height map toward the lamp: the brush ridges of an oil sketch, a plate mark, an embossed fern and a blind-stamp in paper that look blank in flat light, the wedges in a clay tablet, or your own photo. The pointer's direction from the centre is the light's direction and its distance from the rim is its height, so moving in raises the light and flattens the shadows; the direction follows on springs.glide, the height on springs.drift, a click sets the lamp down with the marker landing on springs.recoil, and the first time it is seen the light comes down from overhead and the relief rises out of a flat picture. On the keyboard, Left and Right orbit the lamp and Up and Down raise and lower it.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/raking-light`

Props:
- `subject`: "canvas" | "paper" | "tablet" (default "canvas") — The object on the table, drawn in code: an oil sketch, a sheet of embossed paper or a clay tablet.
- `src`: string — Your own photograph to relight instead (it must be readable across origins). Its height comes from depthSrc, or from its brightness.
- `depthSrc`: string — A depth map for src, white for high, black for low.
- `alt`: string — What the image shows, for assistive technology. Each subject has its own description by default.
- `inscription`: string (default "COLD PRESSED · MADE BY HAND · NO. 14 ·") — The words pressed around the paper's blind-stamp.
- `elevation`: number (default 12) — The raking angle: how many degrees above the surface the light skims when it lies at the edge, 2 to 40.
- `relief`: number (default 0.6) — How tall the surface's ridges stand, 0 (flat print) to 1 (deep relief).
- `warmth`: number (default 0.55) — The light's colour, 0 (cool north daylight) to 1 (warm tungsten); the shadows fill with the other.
- `softness`: number (default 0.35) — The lamp's size, 0 (a pin-point with crisp shadows) to 1 (a softbox with soft ones).
- `gloss`: number (default 0.4) — How much the surface glints where it faces the light, 0 (matte) to 1.
- `azimuth / defaultAzimuth`: number (default 290) — The direction the resting light comes from, degrees clockwise from the top; controlled or uncontrolled.
- `onAzimuthChange`: (azimuth: number) => void — Fires when a click, a tap or the arrow keys set the light down in a new direction, in whole degrees.
- `onLightChange`: (light: { azimuth: number; elevation: number; held: boolean }) => void — Fires as the hand moves the lamp, with the light it is asking for, in whole degrees.
- `intro`: boolean (default true) — The light comes down from overhead to its raking angle the first time the object is seen.
- `showLamp`: boolean (default true) — Show a small lamp where the light comes from while it is held.
- `interactive`: boolean (default true) — The pointer and the keyboard move the lamp.
- `seed`: number (default 1) — Seeds the brushstrokes, the paper's fibres and the wedges in the clay.
- `dpr`: number (default 2) — Cap on the canvas's device pixel ratio, at most 2.
- `label`: string (default "Lamp") — The accessible name of the lamp control.
- `className`: string (default "h-56 w-full") — Sizes and shapes the box.

Notes:
- Give the box a height (the default is h-56 w-full). The object is laid out for the box's own aspect and baked once — on first sight, and again only when the subject, seed, inscription, image, palette or size changes (size changes wait 140 ms for the resize to stop).
- Keyboard: one focus stop. Left and Right orbit the lamp 15° (PageUp and PageDown 45°) and set that direction as the rest; Up and Down raise and lower it, Home lays it low and End lifts it overhead; blur lets it sink back to elevation. A polite live region reads the light once the keys settle.
- Pointer: hovering holds the lamp, a click sets it down facing that way (onAzimuthChange), leaving lets it sink back. On touch, a sideways drag moves the lamp and lifting the finger sets it down; an upright swipe still scrolls the page.
- Reduced motion: no intro and no springs — the light goes straight where the pointer or keys put it and sinks back at once; the object is still fully relit, because direction and height are information.
- Cost: one fullscreen WebGL2 draw per frame only while the light moves, none when settled, off screen or in a hidden tab; the height buffer is half-float where it can be rendered, DPR capped at dpr. Without WebGL2, or after a lost context, a CSS still of the object washed from the resting side stays.
- Bring your own photo with src (and depthSrc for a real depth map); it must be same-origin or served with CORS, and if it cannot be read the drawn subject is shown instead. The subjects' colours are pigments at fixed lightness, so they look the same in either theme.

### Monospace Pond (KQ-1896) — `monospace-pond`
A paragraph you can stir like still water.

A paragraph of monospaced text that is also the surface of a pond: the words stay real, selectable DOM text, and a canvas redraws every character from a glyph atlas where the page laid it out, riding a damped wave equation simulated one character wide with walls that reflect. Swells shoulder the letters toward their crests and lift them, the crests turn them into denser glyphs from the ramp in the crest's ink while troughs thin the ink, and when the energy is gone the original text is drawn exactly again. The pointer drags a trough and its wake through the water as hard as it is quick; a click, a tap, Enter or keyboard focus drops a stone that falls, dents the surface and rings outward under a hairline ring while a crown of droplet glyphs hops out, and the arrow keys move a fingertip that glides between characters on springs.snap while Escape smooths the water away on springs.glide.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/monospace-pond`

Props:
- `text`: string (default a short reservoir note (MONOSPACE_POND_TEXT)) — The paragraph. Line breaks in it are kept; spaces wrap as usual.
- `as`: "p" | "div" | "blockquote" (default "p") — The element the paragraph renders as.
- `damping`: number (default 0.35) — How quickly the water settles, 0 (rings for seconds and rebounds off the edges) to 1 (settles like syrup).
- `ramp`: "ascii" | "blocks" | "dots" | "marks" | string (default "ascii") — The glyphs a crest turns letters into, light to dense: a named ramp or your own string.
- `depth`: number (default 0.5) — How deep the pond is, 0 to 1: deeper water carries waves faster and bends the letters further.
- `stir`: number (default 0.6) — How hard the pointer drags waves through the text, 0 to 1.
- `radius`: number (default 2.5) — The pointer's footprint in characters, 1 to 6.
- `stone`: number (default 0.7) — How big a dropped stone is, 0 to 1.
- `crest`: number (default 0.5) — How readily crests swap letters for ramp glyphs, 0 (only the highest) to 1 (any swell).
- `foam`: boolean (default true) — Word gaps froth with the lightest glyph on strong crests, so a ring reads across them.
- `ring`: boolean (default true) — A hairline ring rides out from every stone with the wavefront.
- `color`: string (default "var(--foreground)") — The ink of the text at rest.
- `crestColor`: string (default "var(--accent-bright)") — The ink the crests, the foam and the ring mix toward.
- `interactive`: boolean (default true) — The pointer, touch and keyboard disturb the water.
- `paused`: boolean (default false) — Freeze the water where it is; it ignores the hand until unpaused.
- `intro`: boolean (default true) — One stone drops by itself the first time the paragraph is seen.
- `seed`: number (default 1) — Where the intro stone falls and how a stone's droplets fly.
- `dpr`: number (default 2) — Cap on the canvas's device pixel ratio, at most 2.
- `label`: string (default "Stir the water") — The pond's accessible name.
- `onStone`: (at: { line: number; column: number }) => void — Fires for every stone a click, a tap, Enter or keyboard focus drops, with its line and column (from 0).
- `onCalmChange`: (calm: boolean) => void — Fires when the water starts to move (false) and when it is still again (true).
- `className`: string — Sizes the box and sets its type: the font size is inherited.

Notes:
- The paragraph is the real text — read once by assistive technology, selectable and copyable; the canvas under it is aria-hidden and only takes over drawing once it is ready, so the server render and any failure show plain text.
- Keyboard: the pond is one focus stop (role group, roledescription pond). Focus drops a gentle stone where the fingertip rests; Left and Right move the fingertip a character, Up and Down a line, Home and End to the line's ends, stirring as it goes; Enter or Space drops a stone; Escape smooths the water away (and is left alone when the water is already still).
- Reduced motion: nothing travels and nothing is displaced. A stone leaves a still ring of swapped glyphs and a hairline ring that cross-fade back to the text; the pointer leaves the text alone.
- Cost: the water is a few thousand cells stepped at 120 Hz and the text a few hundred atlas draws a frame, only while the water moves, on screen and in a visible tab; settled, it draws the clean text once and stops. Layout and atlas rebuild on resize, font load and colour change; DPR capped at dpr.
- Type: the font size is inherited and padding is in em, so it works from a caption to a lead paragraph. Positions come from the page's own layout, so any font works, though the swapped glyphs line up best in a monospaced one. Colours default to tokens and re-read on a theme change.

### Spur Columns (KQ-2050) — `spur-columns`
Follow any phrase into its own column.

An assistant thread where any phrase becomes its own column: choose a dotted phrase in an answer, or select any words and ask about them, and the phrase is lifted out as a chip and carried to the new column's header on springs.glide — landing exactly, because the destination comes from the computed layout rather than a mid-flight measure — while the new column grows in and the older ones narrow to readable spines on the same spring. Every column has its own skeleton, empty and failed states and its own follow-up composer, answered through answerFor (which may return a promise). Left and Right walk the columns, Escape folds the rightmost back into its phrase on the exit ease and returns focus there, and under 520px the columns become a stack that follows a sideways swipe 1:1, rubber-bands at the ends and commits by projection with the trail shown as chips.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/spur-columns`

Props:
- `columns / defaultColumns`: SpurColumn[] (default — / defaultSpurColumns) — Columns left to right, controlled or initial: { id, phrase?, parentId?, turns: { id, prompt, status: "loading" | "ready" | "empty" | "failed", answer?: { text, phrases? } }[] }.
- `onColumnsChange`: (columns) => void — Fires with every column after an open, a fold, an ask or an arriving answer.
- `answerFor`: (prompt, context) => SpurAnswer | null | Promise<…> (default defaultSpurAnswerFor) — Answers a spur's phrase or a follow-up ({ columnId, phrase?, kind: "spur" | "ask" }). null shows the empty state; a rejected promise shows the failed state with Try again.
- `onAsk`: (text, columnId) => void — A follow-up was asked in a column's composer.
- `onOpenSpur`: (phrase, fromColumnId, column) => void — A spur was opened from a suggested phrase or a selection.
- `onCloseSpur`: (columnId) => void — A spur, and any spurs opened from it, was folded back (Escape or its close button).
- `active / defaultActive`: string (default — / the last column) — The active column id, controlled or initial. The active column always stays open.
- `onActiveChange`: (columnId) => void — Fires from the key, spine, chip, phrase or swipe that changed the active column.
- `columnWidth`: number (default 280) — The width older open columns hold, in px — the newest column takes the rest — and the width a column needs to stay open; columns that no longer fit narrow to spines, oldest first.
- `spineWidth`: number (default 40) — A spine's width in px.
- `spineStyle`: "label" | "index" | "bar" (default "label") — Spines read their phrase set vertically, show a large number with a dot per turn, or a slim accent bar under the number.
- `accent`: string (default "var(--accent-bright)") — Phrase marks, the carried chip, spines, the active column's edge, trail chips and Send — any CSS colour.
- `stackBelow`: number (default 520) — Below this container width (px) the columns become a swipeable stack with a trail of chips.
- `allowSelection`: boolean (default true) — Selecting words in an answer offers "Ask about this" above the selection.
- `maxPhrase`: number (default 64) — The longest selection, in characters, that can become a spur.
- `title`: string (default "Fernworks onboarding") — The first column's heading and the region's name.
- `status / onRetry`: "ready" | "loading" | "error" / () => void (default "ready") — Loading shows skeleton columns; error shows a message and Try again, which calls onRetry.
- `height`: number (default 540) — The surface's height in px; each column scrolls inside it.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — Read only: columns can be walked and read; nothing can be opened, folded or asked.
- `className`: string — Classes for the outer section.

Notes:
- Keyboard: suggested phrases are buttons ("Ask about SSO") — the keyboard path to a spur; Left and Right walk the columns and focus each header; Escape folds the rightmost spur and returns focus to the phrase it came from. On a phone the trail chips are tabs.
- Answers can be async: return a promise from answerFor and the column shows a skeleton until it settles; resolve null for the empty state, reject for the failed state with Try again.
- Reduced motion: no chip flight, no width glides and no stack slide — headers appear, columns resize at once and the skeleton does not shimmer; phrase marks and column numbers still show.
- Nothing runs at rest: one ResizeObserver reads the container, the layout is computed from it, and the skeleton's shimmer exists only while a column is loading.
- The layout follows its container: from stackBelow up it is a row of columns and spines; below it, a stack that follows the finger 1:1 with touch-action pan-y so vertical scrolling inside a column still works.

The product as a spec sheet: capabilities set like a chassis plate — grouped terms, mono values, one plain note each — rows resolving on the cascade as the plate enters. For readers who trust a specification more than an adjective, which is most of the readers worth having.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/features-spec-sheet`

Props:
- `groups`: SpecGroup[] — Heading plus term/value/note rows per group.
- `plateLine`: string — The stamped footer line on the plate.

Notes:
- Values are mono and short; the note underneath carries the prose.
- Every line should be checkable — the copy promises lines come off the plate when untrue.
- The double border is the plate's chassis; keep it.

### Gauge Row Features (KB-261) — `features-gauge-row`
A needle at two-thirds beats an adjective.

Capability as headroom: three needle gauges from the library's own cluster, swept to bench-condition values with their red zones showing — because a needle sitting at two-thirds with a visible redline says more about capacity than any adjective. Two notes below say what the reader is looking at and why the honesty is the feature.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/features-gauge-row`

Props:
- `gauges`: Gauge[] — The cluster's needles — value, max, unit, redline.
- `notes / attestation`: GaugeNote[] · string — What the reader is looking at, and the bench conditions.

Notes:
- Needle sweep, red zones, and meter semantics belong to gauge-cluster.
- Set values at honest load — needles pinned at 10% read as staged.
- The attestation names the conditions; gauges without conditions are theatre.

### Signature Line CTA (KB-262) — `cta-signature-line`
Joining as a public act.

The close as a signature line: a ledger of names instead of an email funnel — the count rolls, the latest signatures sit there as provenance, and signing asks only for a name. For communities and open registries where joining is a public act, and the page's proof is who already did.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/cta-signature-line`

Notes:
- Signing asks for a name only — adding an email field turns it back into a funnel.
- The local increment is honest UI, not the record; wire onSign to the real ledger.
- Recent names render in mono italic, like a signature, not a testimonial.

### Postscript CTA (KB-263) — `cta-postscript`
The page stops presenting and starts talking.

The close as a postscript: after the whole page has argued, one short paragraph in the founder's voice — set like the end of a letter, signed, with a single action and one quiet alternative. It works because it drops the register: the page stops presenting and starts talking.

Notes:
- Keep it under four sentences or it becomes another section.
- The alternative is an inline text link on purpose — two buttons would raise the register again.
- Write the P.S. in a person's voice; the drop in register is the device.

### Seat Counter Pricing (KB-264) — `pricing-seat-counter`
See where the next seat gets cheaper.

Seat pricing with the arithmetic on the counter: step the seats and both numbers roll — the applicable rate, which drops at printed breaks, and the total it produces. Discrete where the usage dial is continuous: for teams who buy in people, not units, and want to see exactly where the next seat gets cheaper.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/pricing-seat-counter`

Props:
- `breaks`: SeatBreak[] — Ascending rate breaks; the active one reads full strength.
- `min / max / defaultSeats`: number — The counter's range.
- `onCta`: (seats, total) => void — Fired with the counted crew and its total.

Notes:
- Stepping belongs to stepper-number — keyboard, hold-to-repeat, and clamping come with it.
- The applicable rate is the whole-count rate, not banded — print the breaks so that is obvious.
- Both numerals are readouts; a break crossing rolls rate and total together.

### Margin Notes Content (KB-274) — `content-margin-notes`

An editorial passage with its annotations in the margin, aligned to the paragraph each one belongs to — the shape of a marked-up document rather than a marketing page. ### Live Floor Social Proof (KB-275) — `proof-live-floor`
Somewhere it is 06:40.

Proof as the floor itself, running: a live feed of what is happening across every yard right now, arriving on the conveyor with the standing counts above it. Where the evidence band assembles a case from logos, metrics, and a quote, this one makes the simpler and harder argument — that the thing is in use at this moment, and here is it happening.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/proof-live-floor`

- `counts`: FloorCount[] — The standing numbers above the feed.

Notes:
- Rotation is deterministic — the server renders tick 0 and the client walks the same pool, so there is no hydration drift and no clock.
- Each arrival gets a fresh row key; reusing an event id would read to the conveyor as a reorder, not an arrival.
- Never name customers in the feed. Coarse places are proof; a customer list is a leak.
- Ages come from row position, not timestamps — nothing here needs to be true to the second to be honest.

### Ring Set Stats (KB-289) — `stats-ring-set`
Comparable at a glance, defined in plain words.

Four proportions on one scale, read as wedges rather than numerals: the radial set makes shares comparable at a glance in a way four separate percentages never are, and every wedge carries a plain sentence saying what it counts. It wants values with real spread — four numbers inside a twenty point band are indistinguishable as wedges.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/stats-ring-set`

Props:
- `data / max`: RadialBar[] · number — The wedges and the value that reaches the outer radius.
- `notes`: RingNote[] — One plain sentence per wedge saying what it counts.

Notes:
- All four values must be shares of the same population, or the shared scale lies.
- A percentage without a definition is decoration — the notes column is not optional.
- Give it spread. Values inside a twenty point band render as four wedges of the same length, and the section stops making its own argument.
- Let the weakest number in; four numbers above ninety persuade nobody.

### Incident Log Trust (KB-290) — `trust-incident-log`

### Not For You Use Case (KB-292) — `usecase-not-for-you`
Name the misfits and send them elsewhere.

The use-case section that also says who it is not for — and sends those readers somewhere else by name. Pages that only list good fits leave the reader to work out the bad ones alone, usually after a trial and a disappointment. Naming the misfits costs a few unqualified signups and buys every remaining claim its credibility.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/usecase-not-for-you`

Props:
- `goodFits / badFits`: FitCase[] — Both lists, at equal weight.
- `instead`: string — Where a misfit should go instead — the line that makes it generous rather than coy.

Notes:
- Every bad fit needs an `instead`, or the column reads as false modesty.
- Make the misfits real. A 'not for you' list of strawmen is worse than no list.
- Keep both columns the same length; an unbalanced pair looks like hedging.

### Job Stories Use Case (KB-293) — `usecase-job-stories`
Situations, not job titles.

Use cases written as job stories rather than personas: the situation, the motivation, the outcome — and then, unusually, the single thing in the product that serves it. A job story without that last line is a nice sentence about a customer; with it, the section becomes a map from circumstance to feature the reader can check.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/usecase-job-stories`

Props:
- `stories`: JobStory[] — When / want / so-that, plus the thing that serves it.
- `servedLabel`: string — Caption over the serving line.

Notes:
- The `served` line is what separates this from a wall of nice sentences — never leave it out.
- Write situations, not roles: the same person wants different things at different hours.
- The connectives are set in the muted ink so the story reads as one sentence, not three fields.

### Who Does What How-It-Works (KB-294) — `how-who-does-what`
A division of labour, committed to.

How it works, answered as who does the work: three lanes — your side, the product, and ours — with each step in the lane that owns it. Most how-it-works sections quietly imply the reader does everything or nothing; this one commits to a division of labour, which is what a buyer is really asking when they ask how long it takes.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/how-who-does-what`

Props:
- `steps`: HandoffStep[] — Each step's owning lane, copy, and effort line.
- `lanes`: Record<LaneOwner, string> — Lane names: your side, the product, ours.

Notes:
- The effort line is the honest part — a lane diagram without durations answers nothing.
- Lanes collapse below md and each step names its own owner inline, so nothing depends on column position at 360.
- Give your own team real steps. Three lanes where one is empty is a two-lane diagram with a decoration.

### Plain Steps How-It-Works (KB-295) — `how-plain-steps`
Readable in eight seconds.

Three steps, numbered, and nothing else. The clock, the script, the station line and the lanes all do something with the sequence; sometimes a page has already spent its interaction budget and how-it-works simply has to be read in eight seconds. This is that section, and its restraint is the feature.

- Three steps. If the process genuinely needs five, it needs a different section.
- The standfirst copy is optional here; the headline and the steps are usually enough.

### Segment Shelf Logo Cloud (KB-296) — `logo-segment-shelf`
Anyone like me?

The logo wall organised by trade, with the count each mark stands in for. ### Receipt Wall Logo Cloud (KB-297) — `logo-receipt-wall`
Six with receipts beat thirty without.

A logo wall where every mark carries the number it earned. Bare wordmarks ask the reader to assume the relationship went well; a mark with a measured result attached makes the far stronger claim, and the customer had to agree to the number as well as the name.

### Ship Note Announcement (KB-298) — `announce-ship-note`
Publish the fixes in the same voice as the features.

The week's shipping note as a strip between sections: a version, a date, and three lines that say what actually changed — tagged new, changed, or fixed, with the fix shown rather than hidden. ### Scheduled Window Announcement (KB-299) — `announce-scheduled-window`
The unwelcome notice, done calmly.

The announcement nobody wants to make, made well: a scheduled window with what will actually stop, what will keep working, and why — in that order, because the second list is the one that decides whether anyone has to change their morning.

Notes:

### No Matches Empty State (KB-300) — `empty-no-matches`

The usual empty result leaves you to guess; this hands over the arithmetic.

### Branching Intake Step Form (KB-302) — `stepform-branching-intake`

A branching intake: the first answer decides the route, and the rail visibly re-forms to the length that route actually takes — two stages, or three, or one. ### Resume Later Step Form (KB-303) — `stepform-resume-later`

### Founders Note Team (KB-304) — `team-founders-note`

### Principles List Content (KB-306) — `content-principles-list`
A principle without a cost is a value.

Operating principles with the price of each one attached. Any company can publish four admirable sentences; a principle only becomes information when it says what it costs the people who wrote it — the office view that stays plain, the mornings that arrive flagged, the customers who leave easily.

### Grouped Rollup Table (KB-310) — `datatable-grouped-rollup`

### Inline Edit Table (KB-311) — `datatable-inline-edit`
